passages.text: Ceftazidime prescription and antibiotic resistance patterns in a tertiary care hospital

Ceftazidime, a third-generation cephalosporin, is effective for treating infections caused by gram-negative bacteria. However, increasing antibiotic resistance, particularly in multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacilli, complicates treatment decisions and patient outcomes. This study aimed to assess the clinical epidemiology and characteristics of patients treated with intravenous ceftazidime and clarify the drug resistance patterns of the isolated pathogens. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary care center in the West Bank between June 2021 and June 2023. The study included 558 inpatients across various departments. The data collected included patient demographics, comorbidities, indications for ceftazidime use, dosage regimens, treatment outcomes, and microbiological findings. The demographic and clinical profiles of 558 patients revealed a diverse age distribution, with 57.3% aged 19-65 years. Males constituted 53.2% of the sample. Hematological malignancies (55%) and cardiovascular diseases (32.1%) were the predominant comorbidities. Ceftazidime was predominantly used in oncology settings (68.5%), with neutropenic fever (39.6%) and pneumonia (35.7%) being the most common indications. Discharge was the most common outcome (91.6%), whereas antibiotic interventions, including upgrading therapy (19.4%), were reported. Notably, Escherichia coli was the most isolated pathogen (36.1%), with 47.2% of the isolates demonstrating resistance to ceftazidime. Solid malignancies, diabetes mellitus, and liver disease were significantly associated with poorer outcomes (p < 0.05). Neutropenic fever was linked to better outcomes, whereas pneumonia and sepsis were strongly associated with death. A total of 87.4% of patients developed sepsis or septic shock during treatment (p < 0.05). This study investigated the use of ceftazidime, especially in oncology settings, in a tertiary care hospital. The increasing resistance rate to ceftazidime:particularly among Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae:poses a major challenge for empirical therapy and underscores the urgent need for antimicrobial stewardship in resource-limited settings. Patient age, comorbidities, and infection type significantly influence outcomes, underscoring the need for careful risk stratification. These findings highlight the importance of locally adapted treatment guidelines, routine microbiological surveillance, and further research to optimize antibiotic use and improve patient outcomes.
Background

Antibiotic resistance has emerged as one of the most pressing global health threats, compromising the effectiveness of many first-line antibiotics. The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared antimicrobial resistance (AMR) a global priority, particularly with the rise of multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria. Ceftazidime, a widely used third-generation cephalosporin, is often employed to treat hospital-acquired infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. However, its efficacy is being undermined by increasing rates of resistance, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where empirical therapy is common and antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) may be limited.

Antimicrobial resistance in gram-negative pathogens is often mediated by extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) and carbapenemases, which inactivate beta-lactam antibiotics, including third-generation cephalosporins. A 2024 study from Lebanon reported ceftazidime resistance in more than 60% of Acinetobacter baumannii isolates. In Saudi Arabia and Jordan, Klebsiella pneumoniae and E. coli isolates have shown high levels of ceftazidime and multidrug resistance.

In Palestine, recent studies by Rabayah et al.. and Joudeh et al.. reported a rising burden of ESBL-producing organisms among oncology and febrile neutropenia patients. These findings highlight the urgent need to evaluate local resistance patterns and optimize the use of ceftazidime as empirical therapy.

This study was designed to address this critical issue by focusing on three main objectives: (1) to determine the rate and patterns of resistance to ceftazidime among hospitalized patients in a tertiary care center in Palestine; (2) to evaluate the frequency and type of antibiotic stewardship interventions (e.g., escalation or de-escalation) related to ceftazidime use; and (3) to assess clinical outcomes, including sepsis, mortality, and potential adverse effects, in patients who received empirical ceftazidime therapy.

This issue is particularly relevant in the Palestinian context, where healthcare providers face daily challenges related to medication shortages, limited access to newer broad-spectrum antibiotics, and delays in diagnostic testing. Owing to restricted movement, political instability, and import constraints, many hospitals rely heavily on empirical treatment protocols using available agents such as ceftazidime. The lack of local antibiogram data and the underdevelopment of ASPs further complicate antibiotic selection. These contextual factors underscore the urgency of examining local resistance trends and evaluating the clinical appropriateness of commonly prescribed antibiotics.

The current study investigated ceftazidime prescription patterns in a well-known Palestinian hospital. We aimed to determine what indications and infections it is prescribed for and how often it is prescribed. Additionally, we aimed to study the demographic and clinical characteristics of patients managed with ceftazidime, patient outcomes, and microbiological profiles of the isolated pathogens. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of its kind in Palestine, and it will help physicians prescribe ceftazidime more effectively. In addition to being the first national evaluation of ceftazidime resistance and prescribing patterns, this study uniquely integrates clinical outcomes, ASP interventions, and microbiological data to provide a comprehensive picture of ceftazidime use in a real-world tertiary care setting. Unlike prior regional studies that have focused mainly on microbiological resistance patterns, our study is the first in Palestine to integrate prescribing patterns, clinical outcomes, ASP interventions, and microbiological data into a single analysis. This holistic approach provides novel insights into how ceftazidime is used in a real-world tertiary setting and its implications for AMR management.
Methods
Study design and timing

This study involved a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of patient records at An-Najah National University Hospital (NNUH), which is a tertiary academic hospital in Palestine that serves complex surgical, solid malignancy and hemato-oncological cases. This institution comprises a total of 135 beds. This research focused on assessing the clinical epidemiology and characteristics of patients who received IV ceftazidime between June 2021 and June 2023. Medical records from June 2021 to June 2023 were analysed for patients who received intravenous ceftazidime. Data from 558 inpatients across various hospital departments were examined, excluding outpatient settings.
Study population and sample size

All patients of all ages and sexes who received IV ceftazidime in inpatient settings (surgical, medical, pediatric, cardiac, intensive care unit, bone marrow transplant, cardiovascular surgery, or internal) were included. We excluded outpatient settings, hemodialysis center, and patients who received targeted ceftazidime therapy. The sample size for the study was calculated through a predetermined analysis to ensure both adequate statistical power and representativeness. Using the Raosoft sample size calculator, with parameters of a 50% response distribution, a 0.05 margin of error, and a 95% confidence level, we determined that a minimum of 377 patients were needed. To increase the reliability and statistical power of the study, we decided to enrol 558 patients.
Primary and secondary outcomes

The main aim of this study was to evaluate the prescription pattern of ceftazidime, including the indications for ceftazidime use, duration of therapy, dosage administered, and patient outcomes. However, the secondary goal was to study microbiological profiles, including microbial resistance patterns to ceftazidime, in addition to the occurrence of sepsis or septic shock among patients receiving empirical ceftazidime (the occurrence of sepsis or septic shock was recorded if it developed during hospitalization following ceftazidime administration), along with the length of hospital stay.
Data collection and analysis

This study can be classified as a descriptive study that involved retrospective analysis of patient records to assess the outcomes and usage patterns of intravenous ceftazidime without implementing a controlled experimental environment. We gathered key variables from existing studies and compiled them into Excel spreadsheets, using a format similar to that of studies conducted in our settings. The records of patients who received IV ceftazidime were reviewed at each admission, and the data collection form included the following sections:
Section 1 included the patient's age, sex and admission ward.
Section 2 included information on comorbidities such as hematological malignancies, cardiovascular disorders, solid malignancies, diabetes mellitus, kidney disease and liver disease.

Section 3 describes the different indications for IV ceftazidime use, including neutropenic fever, pneumonia, fever, and sepsis (according to SIRS criteria: body temperature above 38  C or below 36  C, heart rate greater than 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate greater than 20 beats per minute or carbon dioxide partial pressure below 4.3 kPa, and neutrophilia above 12000/mm3 or neutropenia below 4000/mm3 with 10% or more nonsegmented peripheral blood neutrophils), urinary tract infection, soft tissue infection, bacteremia, intra-abdominal infection, surgical prophylaxis, tonsillitis, meningitis, peritonitis, pharyngitis, acute otitis media, cholangitis, encephalitis, endocarditis, and sinusitis. Additionally, it included patient distribution across hospital wards.

Section 4 describes the relationship between patient outcomes (discharge versus death) and two key variables: the dosage of ceftazidime (including total daily dose, maximum dose, and minimum dose) and the duration of ceftazidime treatment. Additionally, it provides an overview of the outcome in terms of overall mortality at the current admission (discharged or died) and interventions (stopped, downgraded, or upgraded). In this study, 'downgrading' refers to switching from ceftazidime to a narrower-spectrum antibiotic, whereas 'upgrading' refers to switching to a broader-spectrum antibiotic on the basis of clinical judgement or microbiological findings. The usual dose of intravenous ceftazidime in our hospital setting is 1-2 g every 8-12 h for adults, with pediatric doses adjusted according to body weight and renal dose adjustment for patients with renal impairment.

In Section 5 the source of infection, specific microorganisms isolated from patients receiving IV ceftazidime, the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and sensitivity to ceftazidime were collected.
Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Descriptive statistics were applied to summarize patient sociodemographic characteristics, medical history, disease comorbidities, and current admission status. Continuous variables such as age, length of hospital stay, dose, and treatment duration were summarized using either the mean and standard deviation or the median and interquartile range (IQR) on the basis of the distribution of the data. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages. To evaluate associations between categorical variables, the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test was applied, with a p value of less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. For data that were not normally distributed, as verified by the Shapiro-Wilk test, the median was used as a more appropriate measure of central tendency. Consequently, the Mann-Whitney test was employed when comparing two groups.
Microbiological identification

Bacterial identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing were performed via the VITEK  2 Compact automated system (bioMerieux, Marcy l'Etoile, France). The identification of bacteria was performed with a VITEK  2 Gram-Negative (GN) identification card. For antibiotic susceptibility testing, AST-N419 cards were used for Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter species, whereas AST-N417 cards were used for various Enterobacterales species. ESBL production and carbapenem resistance were also determined via the VITEK  2 Compact system.
Ethical considerations

The study protocol, which involved accessing and utilizing patient clinical data, received approval from the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) at An-Najah National University (PharmD.Sep.2022/28). Additionally, authorization to access patient files was obtained from An-Najah National University Hospital. Given the retrospective design of the study and the use of anonymized data, the IRB of An-Najah National University waived the requirement for informed consent. All research activities were conducted in accordance with the principles set forth in the Declaration of Helsinki and in compliance with applicable guidelines and regulations. Data confidentiality was strictly maintained, and the information was exclusively used for clinical research purposes. To protect patient privacy, identifiable data were replaced with numerical codes throughout the study.
Results
Demographics and clinical profile of patients treated with IV Ceftazidime

A total of 558 patients were analysed across various age groups and demographic factors. The age distribution revealed that 22.9% were younger than 19 years and that 19.7% were older than 65 years. The sex distribution revealed that 53.2% of the patients were males and that 46.8% were females. Hematological malignancies were present in 55% of the patients, while 32.1% of them had cardiovascular diseases. On the other hand, 28% of them had solid malignancies. The administration of ceftazidime has been observed across various medical departments. The majority of ceftazidime utilization occurred in oncology settings, constituting 68.5% of the cases. Internal medicine accounted for 9.3% of the ceftazidime-treated patients, followed by pediatrics at 8.1%. Detailed demographic data are presented in Table 1.

Indications for IV Ceftazidime use

Among the patients treated with IV ceftazidime, multiple indications have been reported, resulting in 750 instances, reflecting the overlap in indications for some patients, as shown in Table 2. The most common indication for ceftazidime use was neutropenic fever, which occurred in 39.6% of the patients, followed closely by pneumonia in 35.7% of the patients. Fever, as a standalone indication, was noted in 26% of patients.

Clinical interventions involving the Ceftazidime regimen and overall outcomes

Intervention strategies for ceftazidime treatment included stopping treatment due to therapy completion in 276 (49.5%) scenarios, downgrading therapy in 175 (31.4%), and upgrading to another agent in 108 (19.4%). The majority of patients, including 511 (91.6%), were discharged as an overall outcome measure.
Patient outcomes according to the Ceftazidime dosage and duration

The relationships between patient outcomes and the dosage and duration of ceftazidime treatment were evaluated (Table 3). The median total daily dose of ceftazidime was the same for both discharged patients and those who died, with a median of 1 gram (IQR 1-2 g) for both groups (p = 0.709). The duration of ceftazidime treatment also showed no significant difference between the groups (p = 0.985), with both discharged and deceased patients having a median treatment duration of 4 days (IQR 3-6 days).

Associations between outcomes and patient demographics, comorbidities, and infection types

The associations between the primary outcome and patient demographics, comorbidities, and types of infections were analysed in this study. The data revealed that younger age was significantly associated with better outcomes in terms of being discharged (p = 0.000). Among the comorbidities, solid malignancies (p = 0.003), diabetes mellitus (p = 0.022), and liver disease (p = 0.024) were significantly associated with increased mortality. The resistance rate to ceftazidime was also greater in isolates from patients with solid malignancies. However, no significant associations were observed between these comorbidities and pathogen resistance rates to ceftazidime. Neutropenic fever was more common among those discharged (41.1%) than among those who died (23.4%), with a significant p value of 0.018. Pneumonia was significantly more common in those who died (55.3%) than in those discharged (0.8%), with a p value of 0.003. This is illustrated in Table 3.

A total of 87.4% of patients developed sepsis or septic shock during therapy. Among these patients, the mortality rate was 12.6%, which was significantly greater than that of patients who did not develop sepsis or septic shock (p < 0.05). The associations between the duration of hospital stay and the development of sepsis/septic shock among patients treated with ceftazidime are presented in Table 3.
Antibiotics that were upgraded or downgraded from Ceftazidime

In the present study, antibiotic interventions included both downgrading and upgrading treatments. Among the downgraded antibiotics, ciprofloxacin was the most common, constituting 12.2% of the cases; in contrast, piperacillin/tazobactam was the most common antibiotic among the upgraded antibiotics, constituting 11.8% of the cases. Notably, there were overlaps due to multiple upgraded or downgraded antibiotics for some patients, resulting in a total of 196 instances of downgraded antibiotics and 130 instances of upgraded antibiotics within the study population. Isolated microorganism frequency and Ceftazidime susceptibility of patients treated with IV Ceftazidime

We analysed culture results that were tested for ceftazidime and identified a total of 72 pathogens. The largest proportion of samples were urine samples (40.3%), followed by sputum samples (30.5%) and blood samples (16.7%). Other sources included wounds/tissues (7%), fluids (4.2%), and ear samples (1.4%).

A microbiological profile study of patients who were treated with IV ceftazidime revealed that of the total patients, 72 patients had positive cultures tested for ceftazidime susceptibility. Among them, Escherichia coli was the most prevalent (36.1%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae at 19.4% and Pseudomonas aeruginosa at 11.1%. Additionally, the sensitivity of the isolates to ceftazidime was evaluated, with 38 (52.8%) isolates exhibiting sensitivity. Discussion

This retrospective observational study provided insights into the prescription practices of IV ceftazidime at a Palestinian tertiary care hospital, in addition to the microbiological profile of the isolated pathogens in patients treated with this agent. This study revealed that 68.5% of patients treated with ceftazidime were oncology patients. The most common indication for ceftazidime was neutropenic fever (39.6%), which is caused by chemotherapy-induced neutropenia. Ceftazidime is used as a first-line antibiotic for treating high-risk febrile neutropenia patients because of its anti-Pseudomonas properties. The second most common indication for ceftazidime was pneumonia (35.7%), which is in accordance with another study conducted in northern Ethiopia in which pneumonia was one of the most common indications (34.3%) 10. Furthermore, a case study in the United States revealed that 41% of patients treated with ceftazidime for pneumonia responded well to the treatment.

Major contributors to hospitalized patient mortality include sepsis and septic shock, which are linked to unacceptably high mortality and long-term morbidity. In our study, 87.4% of the patients experienced sepsis or septic shock following ceftazidime administration during hospitalization. Septic shock was defined according to the Sepsis-3 criteria, and all patients were followed until discharge or death. The highest risk groups included patients < 19 or > 65 years and those with underlying conditions such as solid malignancies, diabetes mellitus, or liver disease. Despite the high incidence of septic shock, in-hospital mortality remains relatively low (8.4%), likely due to early antibiotic initiation, specialized monitoring, and supportive care. Given the high rates of septic shock and ceftazidime resistance, empirical use in critically ill patients should be carefully considered, with culture-guided therapy prioritized.

The microorganisms most frequently isolated from patients treated with ceftazidime were Escherichia coli (36.1%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (19.4%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (11.1%). Among these strains, Escherichia coli presented the highest resistance to ceftazidime, with approximately 20.8% of the isolates being resistant. Overall, 47.2% of the bacterial isolates in our study were resistant to ceftazidime, although only a minority of the patients were culture positive. These resistance rates are comparable to those reported in previous Palestinian studies (2022), where ceftazidime resistance reached 60% in Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from oncology wards. Similarly, in Lebanon (2019) and Jordan (2022), resistance rates ranging from 50 to 70% have been reported for key gram-negative organisms in intensive care patients and hospitalized patients, respectively. This regional consistency highlights a shared AMR burden in the Eastern Mediterranean region and supports calls for region-specific empiric treatment guidelines. This finding aligns with previous regional studies that reported significant resistance among gram-negative bacteria. On the basis of the observed susceptibility patterns, ceftazidime may remain a reasonable empirical choice for certain infections, such as neutropenic fever, although caution is warranted given the overall high resistance rate. These results highlight the importance of considering patient-specific factors, such as medical history, allergies, underlying conditions, type of infection, disease severity, and local resistance patterns, when choosing empirical therapy.

Additionally, nearly one-fourth of the ceftazidime treatments were upgraded. These resistance rates are comparable to those reported in previous regional studies conducted between 2018 and 2022 among oncology and general hospitalized patients in Palestine, Lebanon, and Jordan, highlighting a shared AMR burden in the Eastern Mediterranean region. A Palestinian study reported that 60% of Klebsiella pneumoniae strains were resistant to ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, and piperacillin/tazobactam9. Similarly, 95.5% of Enterobacteriaceae in intra-abdominal infections are resistant. In contrast, a Lebanese study reported increased susceptibility of Acinetobacter baumannii (64.8%) to ceftazidime. A study conducted in the Slovak Republic revealed that Pseudomonas aeruginosa is resistant to ceftazidime and cefepime by 7.7% .

The high resistance rate to ceftazidime indicates the need for combination empiric therapy for patients with suspected resistant pathogens to increase therapeutic effectiveness until the final culture results are available. While ceftazidime has shown efficacy in treating severe cases, its use must be approached cautiously because of the increasing resistance rates observed in serious infections. As highlighted in this study, 47.2% of the isolates were resistant to ceftazidime, and nearly one-fourth of the treatments required escalation. This underscores the importance of careful antibiotic prescription practices to reduce the risk of resistance and treatment failure in critically ill patients.

The clinical implications of these findings are particularly relevant in the Palestinian healthcare setting, where diagnostic delays, limited antimicrobial formularies, and frequent drug shortages necessitate empirical prescribing. The high ceftazidime resistance rate suggests that its continued use as a first-line agent:particularly in critically ill patients:may no longer be appropriate without culture guidance. This highlights the urgent need for structured ASPs to promote local antibiogram use, guide empiric choices, and support timely de-escalation or escalation. For example, a study from Thailand demonstrated that implementing an antimicrobial restriction system significantly increased appropriate carbapenem prescribing (from 38.3% to 55.0%) and reduced carbapenem expenditure by 36%, even without infectious disease consultation. In resource-limited settings such as Palestine, ASPs are particularly critical owing to restricted drug formularies, frequent shortages of broad-spectrum antibiotics, limited access to rapid diagnostics, and reliance on empirical prescribing. Without ASP, inappropriate antibiotic use accelerates resistance and further limits therapeutic options. As part of ASP policies, therapeutic strategies also play a role in containing resistance and providing treatment options for difficult-to-treat pathogens, such as carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae, which was reported in 5.6% of the cases. Studying combination therapy vs. monotherapy efficacy for managing carbapenem-resistant pathogens and the 30-day mortality rate were the aims of a recent study, revealing that a combination therapy did not outperform monotherapy in terms of 30-day mortality or clinical and microbiological responses. Recent studies further support the urgent need for tailored ASP interventions in the region. One study from the Eastern Mediterranean highlighted the high prevalence of ceftazidime-resistant pathogens, emphasizing the role of targeted interventions to curb resistance. Additionally, another study discussed the successful implementation of ASP protocols, which significantly reduced resistance rates in tertiary care settings. Another important aspect of ASP is optimizing the treatment duration. In terms of antimicrobial stewardship, reducing the duration of an antibiotic course may help lower antibiotic resistance. However, a previous study reported that long-course therapy had a lower 30-day mortality rate than short-course therapy did, comparable nephrotoxicity, and higher rates of clinical and microbiological response.

Interestingly, despite the high resistance rates, patients with neutropenic fever:the most common indication for ceftazidime:had relatively low mortality. This may reflect early initiation of antibiotics, specialized oncology care, and frequent reassessment. However, this outcome should not be interpreted as a justification for maintaining current empirical practices; rather, it underscores the need to revise local guidelines to reflect resistance patterns and infection severity.

Specific strategies to enhance ASPs in our setting include the development and regular dissemination of local antibiograms, the implementation of preauthorization policies for high-risk antibiotics, and routine audit-and-feedback sessions involving pharmacists and infectious disease specialists. Educational initiatives targeting prescribers, particularly junior physicians and trainees, are also essential to promote rational prescribing habits. Ongoing education and awareness initiatives are vital for fostering responsible antibiotic prescribing practices. Implementing regular training sessions on ASPs, providing updated guidelines, and incorporating clinical decision support tools into daily practice can significantly reduce inappropriate antibiotic use. Engaging healthcare professionals through feedback mechanisms and multidisciplinary discussions is essential to sustain improvements in prescribing behavior and patient outcomes. Integrating clinical decision support tools into the electronic health records system may further optimize antibiotic selection and dosing.

Several modifications and interventions for ceftazidime were carried out during the study period. Discontinuing ceftazidime was the major intervention (49.5%), followed by downgrading to another narrower spectrum agent (31.4%) and upgrading to another antibiotic (19.4%).

Our findings also revealed that certain comorbidities were significantly associated with worse outcomes in patients receiving ceftazidime. Specifically, solid malignancies, diabetes mellitus, and liver disease are linked to relatively high mortality rates. These conditions may contribute to immune system dysfunction, delayed recovery, or a greater likelihood of severe infections and complications. This finding reinforces the need for careful patient risk stratification when selecting empirical antibiotic regimens. Among these comorbidities, solid malignancies had the strongest association with mortality, with 46.8% of patients with solid malignancies succumbing to their condition. This highlights the significant impact of malignancy-related immune suppression on patient outcomes.
Future research and clinical implications
On the basis of the findings of our study, some recommendations for future research and clinical implications are as follows:

Preventive actions based on the spread of isolates can be derived. Whether ceftazidime prescription settings, such as frequency, administration techniques, and indications, are appropriate should be examined. Prospective analyses that examine the relevant parameters include randomized controlled trials.

The effects of ceftazidime resistance on patient outcomes, including mortality, length of hospital stay, and treatment failure rate, were examined. Studies comparing the efficacy of different treatment approaches, such as targeted therapy versus empirical therapy, can yield valuable data for clinical decision-making and resource allocation. A program for ASP was created and assessed for a Palestinian tertiary care hospital. A successful plan requires a multidisciplinary approach involving physicians, microbiologists, pharmacists, and infection control specialists.

Patient and family participation should be promoted to better understand patients' preferences regarding potential complications. Incorporating shared decision-making principles and patient-reported outcomes into clinical practice can decrease unnecessary antibiotic use and increase treatment adherence and satisfaction.
Strengths and limitations

This study is the first of its kind in Palestine, addressing the topic of clinical epidemiology and microbiology profiling of patients receiving ceftazidime treatment at a tertiary care hospital. This study provides important baseline data to inform empirical antibiotic therapy in the region, particularly in the absence of national surveillance systems. Additionally, the study benefited from its large sample size, comprising data from 558 patients. The retrospective observational nature of this study raises the risk of incomplete or missing information, particularly concerning the susceptibility pattern of the pathogens. Because the data were extracted from past medical records rather than being prospectively collected, some variables may have been underreported. Additionally, causal relationships between resistance and outcomes cannot be inferred from this design. The quality of medical records determines the accuracy and completeness of the data. For example, adverse effects and renal dose adjustments were not feasible. Second, the study's application to other situations or populations may have been limited by the fact that it was carried out at a single tertiary care hospital in Palestine. Third, the study's timeframe from June 2021 to June 2023 may not have adequately captured variations in prescription practices and resistance patterns over different periods. Another limitation is that the factors leading to modifications in ceftazidime management have not been studied specifically. Finally, one of the key limitations of this study is that while we provided data on the overall rate of ceftazidime resistance among isolated bacteria, we did not include a detailed analysis of specific resistance mechanisms, such as the rates of ESBLs or AmpC beta-lactamases. This was due to the study's scope and resource constraints, which prevented a more in-depth investigation into these mechanisms. Future studies should investigate specific resistance mechanisms, such as extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), AmpC beta-lactamases, and carbapenemases, via molecular techniques to better understand local resistance patterns. In addition, the impact of ongoing armed conflict and political instability in Palestine presents unique challenges for the ASP. Medication shortages, restricted access to newer antimicrobials, and limitations in diagnostic infrastructure all hinder the timely initiation of appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Future research is necessary to explore these specific resistance patterns to better inform antimicrobial therapy and resistance management strategies. This study offers important baseline data that can guide future surveillance and policy efforts in Palestine, especially in the absence of a national antibiogram or real-time resistance tracking system.
Conclusions

This study investigated the use and prescription practices of ceftazidime, especially in oncology settings, in a tertiary care hospital. The increasing resistance rate to ceftazidime:particularly among Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae:poses a major challenge for empirical therapy, especially in critically ill patients, and underscores the urgent need for ASP adoption in resource-limited settings. Patient age, comorbidities, and infection type significantly influence outcomes, underscoring the need for careful risk stratification. These findings highlight the importance of locally adapted treatment guidelines, routine microbiological surveillance, and further research to optimize antibiotic use and improve patient outcomes. Future efforts should focus on developing national antibiotic stewardship frameworks and establishing regular antibiogram reporting to guide empirical antibiotic therapy.

passages.text: Surgical Residents' Feedback Perceptions: A Scoping Review on Gaps and Improvements
ABSTRACT
Background

Feedback is a pivotal instrument for learning and performance enhancement in medical and surgical training. Its established importance for resident development, aiming for highly qualified patient care, faces delivery and utilisation challenges, shifting focus to active learner reception. A critical gap exists in understanding surgical residents' perceptions of this essential process.
Objective

This study aims to systematically identify and map available data regarding surgical residents' feedback perceptions during training, thoroughly analysing findings and delineating existing knowledge gaps.
Methods

Following the Arksey and O'Malley and JBI methodology, a comprehensive search across Medline, Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), Directory of Open Access Scholarly Resources (ROAD), Academic Search Premier (ASP), BioMed Central Open Access (BMC) and Wiley-Blackwell (Wiley) included studies on surgical residents' feedback perceptions (attitudes, experiences, values, beliefs, satisfaction and reported impact). Data charting involved both quantitative and qualitative analyses.
Results

Twelve articles (2017-2024), predominantly United States-based, were included. Residents consistently valued feedback for development and confidence, preferring immediate, verbal and face-to-face delivery, ideally during or directly following a procedure. Common concerns included low frequency, lack of specificity or explicit labelling and delayed provision leading to perceived irrelevance. Influential factors encompassed timing, the learning environment, source credibility (senior residents often preferred) and preceptor personal traits. Critically, the direct impact on learning progress and skill development was often underexamined.
Conclusion

The current evidence based on surgical residents' feedback perceptions is limited by methodological heterogeneity, reliance on retrospective designs and insufficient direct measurement of its actual impact. Resident-preceptor perception discrepancies persist, alongside inadequate detail on feedback characteristics. Thus, standardised, comprehensive and impact-focused research is critically needed to enhance surgical training feedback practices, ultimately contributing to improved patient care.

Introduction
Background

Feedback, conceptualised as information derived from direct observation, constitutes a pivotal instrument for learning and performance enhancement within educational contexts, particularly in medical and surgical training. While its precise underlying mechanisms remain somewhat elusive, its significance for resident physicians' training, ultimately aiming at the provision of highly qualified patient care, is well-established.

Historically, the discourse surrounding feedback centred on optimising its delivery:addressing questions of quality, method and timing. However, a notable paradigm shift has occurred, reorienting the focus towards understanding how learners actively receive and effectively utilise the information provided. This evolution has brought prominence to the concept of 'feedforward,' emphasising sustained learning progression and learner engagement. This shift underscores the critical importance of the learner's perspective, recognising that effective feedback transcends mere transmission, necessitating active reception and integration.

The residents' perception of and immediate reaction to feedback is thus as crucial as the chosen methodology or timing of its provision. Medical students and residents frequently report receiving insufficient feedback. Furthermore, discrepancies in feedback perception often exist between residents and faculty members, although some studies indicate areas of shared understanding regarding effective feedback attributes. Factors such as the teacher's credibility, the environment in which feedback is delivered, and the learner's individual experiences significantly influence this perception. Beyond external feedback, the internal, metacognitive feedback generated through self-reflection is paramount for intentional learning and fostering a lifelong learner mindset.

Surgical residents acknowledge feedback as a source of valuable insights for future improvement, noting that its absence can lead to frustration and impact self-confidence. They typically express a preference for immediate, face-to-face verbal feedback, ideally delivered during or directly following a surgical procedure, and value its prompt provision. Nevertheless, it is commonly observed that postoperative (PO) feedback is delivered with less frequency than deemed optimal. The existing scholarly literature on feedback in surgical education is characterised by methodological and contextual heterogeneity, impeding a cohesive and comprehensive understanding of surgical residents' perceptions. Scoping reviews are particularly well-suited to synthesise evidence from such diverse fields. A preliminary search indicates a notable scarcity of scoping reviews specifically addressing surgical residents' perceptions of feedback, thereby highlighting a critical knowledge gap.

Against this backdrop, the present scoping review aims to systematically identify and map available data regarding surgical residents' perceptions of feedback received during their training, analyse these findings, delineate current knowledge gaps and disseminate the research outcomes.
Methods

This scoping review was meticulously designed and executed to ensure robust methodological rigour and transparency, adhering to best practices in evidence synthesis. It followed Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) five-stage framework, encompassing the following: (i) identifying the research question, (ii) identifying relevant studies, (iii) selecting studies, (iv) charting the data and (v) collating, summarising and reporting the results. Consistent with the iterative nature of scoping reviews, minor refinements to the research question and inclusion criteria were made during the study selection and data charting phases to ensure optimal alignment with the emerging evidence. The review's structure aligns with The Joanna Briggs Institute's (JBI) scoping review methodology. The guiding research question for this study was as follows: 'What is known about surgical residents' perceptions of feedback in their training?' The protocol for this scoping review has been previously published.
Search Strategy

The search strategy was conducted on March 15, 2024, by a specialised librarian. Key descriptors included the following: formative feedback, hospital medical staff, teaching, general surgery and perception, along with their Portuguese and Spanish equivalents, covering the period since 2017. Databases consulted were Medline (via PubMed), Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), Directory of Open Access Scholarly Resources (ROAD), Academic Search Premier (ASP), BioMed Central Open Access (BMC) and Wiley-Blackwell (Wiley), using Descritores em Ciencias da Saude (DeCS) and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) as appropriate. The deliberate exclusion of Scopus and Web of Science was based on evidence indicating substantial content overlap with the selected databases, yielding minimal additional relevant articles for considerable effort. This approach aligns with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines and open science principles, while recognising that theoretical saturation is often achieved with four to six comprehensive databases. The complete search strategy is detailed in Appendix S1.
Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Studies were included if their population comprised resident physicians of any surgical specialty:defined broadly to include all surgical residency programmes such as general surgery, neurosurgery, ophthalmology, plastic surgery, cardiothoracic surgery, vascular surgery, urology, gynaecology and otorhinolaryngology:and if they addressed residents' perceptions of feedback. 'Perceptions of feedback' encompassed attitudes, experiences, values, beliefs, satisfaction and reported impact on learning and development. Eligible study types included qualitative and quantitative primary studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, meta-syntheses, books and guidelines, provided they directly focused on surgical residents' feedback perceptions. Publications such as opinions, consensuses, retractions, editorials, websites and advertisements were excluded due to their lack of empirical data on resident perceptions.
Study Selection

Following the exclusion of duplicate articles, titles and abstracts were independently screened by two researchers. An initial calibration exercise with 25 random articles achieved 92% agreement. Full texts of potentially relevant articles were then evaluated by the main researcher. Any disagreements during the selection process were resolved through discussion or by involving additional researchers. Reasons for full-text exclusions are reported in the results. A manual search also led to the inclusion of additional eligible sources not identified by the initial strategy. The study selection process, aligned with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, is fully depicted in Figure 1. A list of included studies is available in Appendix S2 .
PRISMA-ScR flowchart.
Charting the Data

Data from each selected study were charted by the main researcher using a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Recognising the iterative and flexible nature of scoping reviews, the preliminary data extraction instrument outlined in the review protocol was refined during the full-text review phase to comprehensively capture the depth and heterogeneity of information. The refined instrument facilitated a detailed and systematic collection of variables. A comprehensive set of variables was extracted, encompassing study characteristics, feedback attributes (definition, method, delivery, learning domains, timing), residents' perceptions (positive, negative, influencing factors, effectiveness) and feedback's impact on education (learning, skill development, self-confidence and reflection), alongside identified knowledge gaps, implications for practice and suggestions for future research. The complete data extraction tool is presented in Appendix S3.
Synthesis of Results

Both quantitative and qualitative analyses were performed on the extracted data. Quantitative descriptions and statistical analyses were applied to all data. For qualitative parameters, including feedback delivery methodology, learning domains, positive and negative aspects of perception, influencing factors and feedback's impact, all covered topics were systematically listed and then classified.
Results

The initial database search yielded 588 articles. The findings of each database are available in Appendix S4. Following a rigorous selection process, 270 duplicates were removed, and 284 articles were excluded after title and abstract screening. Of the 34 full-text articles reviewed, five met the eligibility criteria. An additional seven articles were included through manual search, resulting in a total of twelve articles for comprehensive review. The reasons for exclusion were thoroughly documented, with common factors including population mismatch (e.g., nonsurgical residents or mixed groups without separate results), conceptual irrelevance (e.g., feedback in surgical education but not its perception) and full-text unavailability. The entire study selection process is illustrated in Figure 1.
Characteristics of Included Studies

The 12 included studies were published between 2017 and 2024 (two in 2017, two in 2018, one in 2019, two in 2020, two in 2022, two in 2023 and one in 2024). The majority (83.4%; n = 10) were conducted in the United States of America, with single studies from Canada and Pakistan. All were primary studies, and the Journal of Surgical Education was the predominant publication source (nine studies). Methodological designs were diverse, comprising five mixed-methods studies, five qualitative studies, one quantitative study and one cross-sectional survey. Surgical specialties of resident participants predominantly included general surgery (nine studies), alongside ophthalmology, neurosurgery, plastic surgery, thoracic surgery and vascular surgery. Postgraduate year (PGY) levels varied, and sample sizes ranged from 7 participants to 83 respondents, with some studies analysing a large number of evaluations (e.g., 2968 entries in Neal et al.). Academic medical centres and university hospitals constituted the primary institutional contexts. A detailed overview is provided in Table 1.

Feedback Characteristics
Feedback Concept, Method and Delivery Methodology

Most studies did not explicitly define 'feedback'; when mentioned, it generally aligned with 'information about a learner's performance intended to improve performance.' Only Kamal et al. (2017) explicitly mentioned multisource feedback (MSF) and learning conversation methods. Feedback delivery methodologies varied considerably, including: MSF or 360  feedback, face-to-face and one-on-one feedback sessions, immediate verbal feedback (often preferred in the operating room [OR] or immediately post-operatively), formal (written), nonverbal interactions, delivery via online tools (such as Surgical Autonomy Programme [SAP] and Surgical Entrustable Professional Activities [SEPAs] evaluations), faculty evaluation comments and structured PO debriefings.
Instrumentation for feedback was frequently unspecified (4/12 articles), characterised as formal/informal (3/12 each), or via specific written instruments (3/12).
Feedback Learning Domains

Feedback explicitly addressed diverse learning domains including: technical skills and operative performance, nontechnical skills (communication, interpersonal skills, collegiality, humanism, professionalism, resource utilisation and reliability), clinical judgement and decision-making, leadership, autonomy and progression towards independence and self-regulated learning and reflection.
Feedback Timing

Most studies (75%; n = 9) focused on feedback provided during the perioperative (PerO) period, with PO feedback being the most prevalent. Other articles referred to feedback delivered at any point during residency. One study noted monthly and semi-annual formal evaluations. Table 2 provides additional details.

Residents' Perceptions of Feedback
Positive Aspects of Perception

Residents consistently perceived feedback as highly valuable and important for development and learning. It was also reported as beneficial for learning and satisfaction with rotations, confidence-boosting (particularly positive feedback), more constructive and valuable when delivered by senior residents and effective for improving self-regulated learning and awareness of strengths/weaknesses. Feedback was generally well received, preferable when verbal and face-to-face (ideally during or immediately after a surgical case) and desired with greater frequency, especially with dedicated and structured time allocation.
Negative Aspects of Perception

Conversely, residents reported concerns including the low frequency of feedback (particularly outside the OR), lack of specificity, clarity, or explicit labelling as 'feedback' and delayed delivery, leading to perceived irrelevance. Feedback was perceived negatively when delivered in an inadequate environment without privacy, without guidance for improvement (which can be unhelpful and detrimental to confidence) and when accompanied by detrimental comments (demeaning, sarcastic, personal attacks). Residents also noticed variability in feedback quality among attendings and that attendings sometimes failed to remember resident performance. Written feedback was perceived as less valuable compared to verbal feedback.
Feedback was perceived negatively when delivered in an inadequate environment without privacy.
Factors Influencing Perception

Several factors were identified as shaping residents' perceptions. Time constraints and competing attending responsibilities affect feedback frequency and quality. When delivered in calm, respectful and collaborative settings, feedback is perceived more positively than that delivered in hostile environments. Senior residents are often perceived as providing more constructive feedback than attending surgeons; with attending personal traits such as kindness, patience, calmness, approachability and respect serving as factors that positively influence perception. The rapport between residents and attendings is reported as crucial in determining feedback quality. Explicit, direct, practical, granular and specific feedback is perceived as higher quality. Immediate verbal PO feedback is considered ideal, while written and delayed feedback is less valued. It was also reported that perceptions may vary between junior and senior residents and the presence or absence of an institutional 'feedback culture' impacts both provision and reception.
Other Specific Aspects of Perception
Comparison of Perceptions (Residents vs. Preceptors)

No consistent correlation was found between residents' and preceptors' perceptions regarding feedback frequency or quality. Nathwani et al. (2017) reported differing ideal practices, while Dedhia et al. (2019) noted agreement on timing and subjective areas, but discrepancies in perceived frequency.
No consistent correlation was found between residents' and preceptors' perceptions regarding feedback frequency or quality.
Immediate Reaction to Feedback
Only Kamal et al. (2017) described residents' immediate reactions, characterising behaviours as friendly, highlighting a gap in the literature.
Data Collection Methodologies for Feedback Perception

Studies employed diverse methods to investigate perceptions. Surveys, questionnaires, semistructured interviews and focus groups were the most prevalent. Video analysis of perceived events and text analysis of comments and evaluations were also utilised.

Impact of Feedback on Resident's Education
Few studies directly measured the impact of feedback, with most reporting general perceptions. However, some key impacts were identified:
Impact on Learning Progress

Kamal et al. reported overall improvement in residents' attitudes and practice, with statistically significant increases in scores post-intervention and specific behavioural changes. Improved self-regulated learning, awareness of strengths/weaknesses and progression of skills and autonomy throughout residency were reported by Go et al..
Impact on Skill Development

This was the most prevalent impact reported, including: development of nontechnical skills, enhancement of operative skills and autonomy and improvement in judgement and decision-making, especially in PO debriefings.
Impact on Self-Confidence
Self-confidence was positively impacted by positive feedback and operative coaching (OC) programmes.
Impact on Reflection/Internal Feedback
Go et al. reported that feedback facilitates reflection, self-regulated learning, helping residents identify strengths and weaknesses for internal reflection and goal setting.

Knowledge Gaps and Implications
Knowledge Gaps Identified by the Study Authors

The two most prevalent gaps were the absence of attending perspectives, which can limit understanding, and the prevalence of single-centre studies, which affect generalizability. Other key gaps included a lack of consensus between faculty and trainees regarding learning needs and high-quality feedback components, challenges in consistent feedback delivery, limited research on leadership-specific feedback, insufficient understanding of operative skill and entrustment progression in coaching programmes, unclear reasons for feedback frequency differences between university and community hospitals and uncertainty regarding whether Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) assessments provide adequate feedback for leadership development.
Implications for Practice

The review's findings suggest attendings should prioritise feedback in preoperative (PreO) and PO phases, institute dedicated and structured feedback sessions and modify PO workflow to incorporate teaching moments. Similarly, institutions should develop faculty programmes for effective feedback delivery, emphasising explicit labelling and safe environments, implement coaching programmes and structured assessment tools like SEPAs, focus on attendings' personal traits and the learning environment to improve operative performance and autonomy and promote a broader 'feedback culture'. Feedback from senior residents should also be leveraged.
Suggestions for Future Research by the Study Authors

Following the identified gaps, the study authors suggest that larger and multicentre studies be conducted to improve generalizability and that faculty and other team members' perspectives be included. They also suggest that future research should evaluate the impact of interventions designed to improve feedback, investigate biases in evaluations, such as those related to gender and race, explore why residents underestimate skills while attendings overestimate autonomy, research more effective methods for teaching and providing feedback and study verbal feedback during operative cases .

Discussion

This scoping review aimed to map the current understanding of surgical residents' perceptions of feedback, identifying key characteristics and literature gaps. Our findings highlight persistent challenges in understanding this crucial aspect of medical education.

A significant observation was the scarcity and methodological heterogeneity of included articles. Despite a broad search, most studies were single-centre, predominantly from the United States, and primarily retrospective. This methodological diversity, encompassing varied designs and assessment approaches, hinders direct comparisons and robust evidence synthesis. The over-reliance on retrospective data introduces recall bias, potentially compromising the accuracy of reported perceptions, contrasting with the more accurate capture offered by prospective studies. The higher number of manually included articles compared to those from the search strategy also suggests potential limitations in current search practices for this evolving field.

The resident sample heterogeneity, particularly in PGY levels and sample sizes (e.g., Lees et al., 2019), further complicates generalizability, as perceptions vary significantly with training progression. Notably, most studies did not explicitly define 'feedback' for participants, potentially affecting the consistency and interpretation of resident perceptions.

Feedback methods were rarely detailed, with verbal and written forms being most common, and specific instruments used less frequently. This lack of standardisation makes it difficult to ascertain effective approaches. While residents prefer timely, direct and explicit feedback, the 'how' of feedback delivery (e.g., specific models like Pendleton) is often missing, impeding the identification of best practices. The prevalent PerO feedback, especially PO, often delayed, contrasts with the recognised importance of PreO and intraoperative (IO) feedback. The perceived lack of time by preceptors to deliver quality feedback highlights a systemic barrier requiring institutional solutions.

Feedback content covered diverse learning domains:cognitive, affective and psychomotor:though rarely all simultaneously. Psychomotor skills, particularly operative performance and technical skills, were most prevalent, reflecting the practical nature of surgical training. However, this emphasis underscores the need for more holistic feedback approaches.

Residents consistently value feedback as crucial for their development and confidence, especially when positive. Key negative perceptions include low frequency, lack of specificity or explicit labelling and delayed delivery. Factors influencing perception include timing, learning environment, source (senior residents often preferred), explicitness, attending traits and institutional culture. Discrepancies between residents' and preceptors' perceptions are common, with residents often under-recognising feedback that preceptors believe they provide. This communication gap suggests a need for improved delivery techniques and a shared understanding of effective feedback.

Many words were used by the residents to describe the feedback effectiveness, but the most common were 'useful', 'direct', 'formative', 'regular' and 'specific'. In a general way, feedback was perceived as more effective by residents when delivered postoperatively ('at the end of the OR'), both verbally and in writing. Nevertheless, when in writing, residents demonstrated preference if it was made using a standard instrument. Some of the instruments used for this purpose were SEPAs evaluations, SAP online assessment tool, OpTrust scores and mini-peer assessment tool (mini-PAT) questionnaire. Though already described in literature, the use of an App-based system for feedback delivery like System for Improving and Measuring Procedural Learning (SIMPL) and Zwisch Me!! was not reported by the studies included in this scoping review. As already demonstrated by Steinhagen et al., the use of an online feedback tool does not necessarily mean an improvement in feedback effectiveness. However, perhaps more than the utilisation of a standardised instrument, an App-based system, or an online feedback tool, the feedback effectiveness increases if the feedback is explicit, objective and direct, which is surely easier to do with one of these instruments.

While many words describe feedback effectiveness, its actual impact was seldom measured. Only Kamal et al. (2017) and Go et al. (2024) prospectively assessed impact on learning and skill development, highlighting improvements in attitudes, self-regulated learning and autonomy. Critically, the impact on patient care quality or learner engagement was largely underexplored, representing a significant gap given feedback's ultimate goal. This deficiency underscores a need to move beyond mere satisfaction to demonstrable behavioural change and improved performance:the 'feedforward' concept. The absence of standardised, validated instruments for assessing resident perceptions remains a methodological limitation.

Identified knowledge gaps point to crucial research directions: the need for larger, multicentre studies, inclusion of faculty perspectives, evaluation of feedback interventions and investigation of biases, exploration of technology-enhanced feedback and investigation of different feedback methods/instruments' effectiveness.
Limitation

This review has important limitations. Firstly, the search strategy was limited to English, Portuguese and Spanish, excluding articles from other languages and cultures. Given that feedback conceptions and practices vary culturally, the findings may not universally represent global feedback perceptions. Secondly, consistent with Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) framework, stakeholder consultation was not undertaken. While the review comprehensively maps the literature, engaging surgical residents, preceptors and experts could have offered additional perspectives and validated interpretations of identified gaps and opportunities. Thirdly, the inherent methodological heterogeneity of the included studies, particularly the predominance of retrospective designs and varied sample sizes, limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions and conduct rigorous comparisons.
Conclusions

This scoping review reveals that while feedback is universally acknowledged as crucial for learning and skill development in surgical education, the current evidence base presents significant limitations. There is a pervasive lack of standardised methods and instruments for both providing and assessing feedback, leading to heterogeneous data and comparison challenges. A critical underemphasis exists on directly measuring the actual impact of feedback on residents' learning outcomes and on the 'feedforward' concept of actionable improvement.

The review also highlights existing discrepancies between residents' and preceptors' perceptions, insufficient detail in describing feedback characteristics and a scarcity of prospective studies, which limits the depth of understanding regarding immediate reactions and the evolution of perceptions over time. Furthermore, the limited cultural diversity in existing literature suggests that current findings may not fully represent global feedback perceptions in surgical education. In summary, this review underscores a critical need for more standardised, comprehensive and impact-focused research to truly understand and enhance feedback practices in surgical training, ultimately contributing to improved patient care.
